Artificial intelligence and Database Management Systems Integration bring 
intelligence, adaptability, and independence in the world of databases. 
Relational database management systems structure the data and have been 
the foundations for implementing them, although they face several 
challenges that have arisen from modern-day environments of computing 
and information processing, such as scalability, real-time processing, the 
incorporation of unstructured data, and capabilities for making proactive 
decisions. As a result, new approaches like NoSQL and NewSQL appeared 
to address various and scalable needs of the applications. AI concepts such 
as Machine learning (ML), Deep learning (DL), and Natural language 
processing (NLP) have brought about improvement of advanced functions 
and optimization of efficiency into current database systems. These are 
self-tuning, query optimization, predictive caching, and natural language 
interfaces that enable a database to work autonomously while offering 
high-performance and reliability service. This paper focuses on the 
traditional and advanced DBMS architectures, the development and 
integration of AI-based DBMS, and other novelties such as federated 
learning and reinforcement-based cache. 
Keywords—Artificial Intelligence, Database Management System, AI-
DBMS Integration, NoSQL, NewSQL, Intelligent Databases, Query 
Optimization.

I. INTRODUCTION

computer program that helps organize and manage 
databases. Its primary function is to make it easier to 
read, modify, delete, and scale data for the purpose 
of analyses, correlations, and data-driven processes. 
DBMSs are computerized tools for organizing and 
storing data. A wide range of actions for data 
modification and database structure oversight are 
available to users on such a system [1]. 
Database architectures now evolve to handle rising 
requirements for extensive data capacities together 
with faster Speeds and Complex data demands. 
Traditional relational database systems functioned as 
standard data storage platforms but today have

II. OVERVIEW OF TRADITIONAL DATABASE 
ARCHITECTURES 
 
A database is a structured system for storing, 
managing, and retrieving data efficiently. Managed 
by a DBMS, it allows users to organize and access 
data for various applications. Traditional databases 
include relational models (using tables and SQL) and 
non-relational models (like document or graph-
based systems). Databases serve industries at all 
levels to support real-time operations by upholding 
data security standards, which facilitate informed 
decision-making for data-driven environments in 
present times. 
Database architectures that function as the core 
structure for handling data management systems 
have 
operated 
for 
several 
decades. 
These 
architectures were intended to work with structured 
data efficiently by employing SQL and standardized 
schemas for data storage and retrieval purposes. 
RDBMSs became the preferred database solution 
because their robust theoretical base merged with 
their data consistency capabilities complemented by 
transaction processing features. These systems 
operated through a client-server system that divided 
data storage elements from application processing

B. 
NoSQL Database 
A collection of pairs (key, value) is what is often 
found in most basic NoSQL databases, which are 
known as key-value stores or huge hash tables. A 
key is a piece of information that specifies the 
location of a value, which may be a string or a 
pointer. The value associated with a certain key (or 
row-ID) might be a set of names and values, such as 
an attribute name in relational databases or a 
column name in SQL databases [12]. The list of pairs 
of names and values is stored as a blob, often as a 
string.  In other words, a key is the only argument 
required for data access operations like get and put 
[13]. The key-value method allows efficient lookups 
since it is reminiscent of basic abstractions like hash 
tables or file systems. Couples (name, value) may 
take several forms, however, and this is crucial to 
keep in mind.  It may not even "come" from the 
same table in the relational data model. However, 
such databases may be severely limited by too 
simplistic 
data models, 
notwithstanding 
their 
efficiency and scalability.  When dealing with 
schema-less databases, NULL values are unnecessary.

III. ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN THE 
CONTEXT OF DATABASES 
 
Combining DBMS with AI is going to be a game-
changer for the computer industry in the years to 
come. To continue developing DBMS technology 
and to effectively use much of AI, AI/DB integration 
is critical, as mentioned in, and it is also critical for 
future 
generation 
computing. 
Research 
and 
development in the domain of AI/DB integration is 
relatively young, despite the fact that both DBMS 
and AI systems, especially expert systems, are well-
established technologies [17]. One of the main 
reasons why these two technologies are being 
integrated is because of the necessity for  
 
the ability to analyses vast volumes of shared 
data for the purpose of knowledge. 
 
effective administration of data and knowledge  
 
intelligent processing of data.  
Along with these considerations, the goal of 
protecting the significant investment that most 
current databases represent was a driving force in 
the development of the Intelligent Database 
Interface (IDI). Therefore, the ability to employ 
existing DBMSs as separate system components was 
a critical design objective for IDI. There have been a 
number of published and researched broad strategies 
for AI/DB integration in the literature.  
A. Extending the AI System 
With the addition of DBMS capabilities, the AI 
system can handle and access massive volumes of 
stored 
data 
efficiently. 
 
In 
most 
cases, 
comprehensive DBMS technology is not used by 
such systems [18]. On the contrary, the AI system 
takes center stage, with DBMS capabilities being 
provided on an as-needed and restricted basis (e.g., 
by implementing just the data access layer) [19]. It is 
also possible to build a knowledge-based system of 
the next generation, such as Logic Data Language 
(LDL). This strategy essentially necessitates "re-
inventing" DBMS technology in one way or another. 
Although these systems usually provide high-tech 
settings and tools for developing applications, it will 
be very difficult, if not impossible, to build apps that 
can access existing databases. This is especially true 
in cases when the database is often accessed and 
updated by more conventional applications. 
B. 
Extending the DBMS System 
This method enhances a DBMS with features that 
allow for the representation and reasoning of 
knowledge, such as PostgreSQL. In this case, the 
DBMS capabilities take centre stage, with the AI 
capabilities being added on an as-needed basis [20]. 
It often has very limited reasoning and knowledge 
representation skills, and it doesn't have the 
advanced settings and tools seen in most AI systems. 
Without a significant amount of work from the 
application developer, such systems cannot directly 
enable the usage of current DBMSs or AI 
applications (such as expert systems). In a way, this 
is the reverse of the earlier strategy.

IV. AI-DRIVEN ENHANCEMENTS IN DATABASE 
SYSTEMS 
 
AI has imparted new features to the database 
management systems (DBMS) including real-time 
analysis [24], predictive analysis and analysis and 
self-governance. DBMS that use AI involve machine 
learning and natural language processing in various 
operations such as query processing, integration of 
the schema and data anomalies. The use of self-
driving database [25], like Oracle’s self-driving 
database has brought a paradigm shift in this field as 
it supports self-tuning, self-securing, and self-
repairing capabilities based on artificial intelligence 
but a number of issues remain. Compliance-focused 
industries have arisen due to the black-box nature of 
the AI algorithms meaning that the auditors cannot 
put their trust into the fact that it is performing the 
task correctly. Moreover, scalability remains a 
critical concern as the data environment shifts to 
distributed with the volume of data increasing 
exponentially, Federated learning has cropped up as 
a solution to concerns of data privacy and 
sovereignty whereby training of the ML models is 
done across distributed nodes. However, challenges 
such as model consistency and computational 
overhead hinder its widespread adoption in database 
systems. These underexplored areas highlight the 
need for further research to bridge technical 
limitations and practical applications

V. LITERATURE REVIEW 
 
This section provides a literature review on 
enhancing database architectures with Artificial 
Intelligence (AI), highlighting best practices and 
emerging challenges. Table III offers a summary of 
the reviewed studies for a clear and concise 
overview. 
Li et al. (2025) the use of AI in architectural design 
and how it affects design efficiency; 92 papers out of 
1810 were chosen for meta-analysis and review after 
screening by ScienceDirect, Web of Science, Scopus, 
and the China National Knowledge Network (CNKI) 
search engines. The findings highlight the promising 
future of AI in many areas of architectural design, 
such as ideation, data analysis, and issue resolution.  
Further uses of AI in the building lifecycle include 
facility maintenance, construction monitoring, and 
predictive analytics [31] 
Wang et al. (2024) the architecture and functions of 
Intelligent Database Management Systems (IDBMS), 
which integrate advanced artificial intelligence (AI) 
technologies 
to 
enhance 
traditional 
database 
management. By addressing the limitations of 
conventional systems, IDBMS aims to improve 
query optimization, resource utilization, and user 
interaction through machine learning, predictive 
analytics, and natural language processing. The 
paper 
outlines 
the 
core 
components 
and 
architectural models of IDBMS, details their 
functionalities, presents case studies demonstrating 
their effectiveness, and discusses future trends and 
challenges in the field [32]. 
Tian et al. (2024) the low database coupling system 
architecture, by building the data microservice 
layer, so the foreground and middle-ground 
microservices no longer access the database directly 
but access the data microservices, and the data 
microservices complete the specific access to the 
database. In the paper, the handling methods of SQL 
syntax translation, database access adaptation, data 
synchronization and other practical problems in data 
microservices are given. The architecture of the 
paper is validated by taking a large-scale digital 
system, the digital power marketing service system, 
as an example [33]. 
Azaliah et al. (2024) the merging of artificial 
intelligence with enterprise architecture frameworks 
like TOGAF, Zachman, and SOA, with an emphasis 
on approaches, advantages, and disadvantages.  The 
research draws on scholarly databases to examine 
articles published between 2018 and 2024 using a 
Systematic Literature Review (SLR) approach. Key 
results include AI's capacity to automate repetitive 
operations for increased operational efficiency, 
promote innovation via strategic alignment, and 
enhance 
decision-making 
through 
data-driven 
insights and predictive analytics.  Significant 
obstacles still exist, nevertheless, such as the need 
for empirical validation, data privacy difficulties, 
and technological integration problems [34].

efficiency, customization, and sustainability. To 
compile this work, a desk review of relevant 
literature was conducted using databases such as 
Science Direct, ISI Web of Knowledge, and Springer.

VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK 
 
The integration of AI into database management 
systems marks a transformative shift from static, 
manually 
managed 
infrastructures 
to 
dynamic, 
intelligent platforms capable of self-optimization, real-
time analytics, and enhanced user interaction through 
technologies like NLP. AI-powered databases offer 
significant advantages in scalability, performance, and 
automation, making them vital for data-centric 
industries in the era of big data and digital 
transformation. However, challenges such as the 
opaque nature of AI models ("black-box" issue) and 
the computational overhead associated with advanced 
techniques like federated learning still present 
limitations. Addressing these concerns is essential for 
the widespread adoption and trustworthiness of next-
generation intelligent database systems. 
Future research should focus on creating more robust 
frameworks that seamlessly integrate advanced AI 
capabilities into all layers of database architecture, 
including query optimization, anomaly detection, and 
autonomous data governance. Moreover, efforts 
should 
be 
directed 
toward 
enhancing 
the 
explainability and transparency of AI decisions within 
DBMS to ensure ethical data use. Another promising 
avenue lies in developing hybrid database models that 
effectively combine the benefits of RDBMS, NoSQL, 
and NewSQL systems, supported by AI-driven 
automation. Additionally, fostering interoperability 
among AI-augmented systems and improving security 
protocols will be critical in addressing the growing 
demands of data-centric and intelligent applications.
